Peacock Throne of the <color=#3366CC>Mughal</color> and <color=#3366CC>Persian</color> emperors. With the advent of scientific interest in birds, many paintings of
birds were commissioned for books.
Among the most famous of these bird artists was <color=#3366CC>John James Audubon</color>, whose paintings of North American birds were
a great commercial success in Europe and who later lent his name to the National Audubon Society. Birds are also

important figures in poetry; for example, <color=#3366CC>Homer</color> incorporated <color=#3366CC>nightingales</color> into his <color=#3366CC>Odyssey</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Catullus</color> used a
<color=#3366CC>sparrow</color> as an erotic symbol in his Catullus 2. The relationship between an <color=#3366CC>albatross</color> and a sailor is the central theme of
<color=#3366CC>Samuel Taylor Coleridge</color>'s <color=#3366CC>The Rime of the Ancient Mariner</color>, which led to the use of the term as a metaphor for a
'burden'. Other <color=#3366CC>English</color> metaphors derive from birds; vulture funds and vulture investors, for instance, take their name
from the scavenging vulture. Aircraft, particularly military aircraft, are frequently named after birds. The predatory nature
of raptors make them popular choices for fighter aircraft such as the <color=#3366CC>F-16 Fighting Falcon</color> and the Harrier Jump Jet,
while the names of seabirds may be chosen for aircraft primarily used by naval forces such as the HU-16 Albatross and
the V-22 Osprey.
Perceptions of bird species vary across cultures. <color=#3366CC>Owls</color> are associated with bad luck, <color=#3366CC>witchcraft</color>, and death in parts of
Africa, but are regarded as wise across much of Europe. <color=#3366CC>Hoopoes</color> were considered sacred in <color=#3366CC>Ancient Egypt</color> and
symbols of virtue in <color=#3366CC>Persia</color>, but were thought of as thieves across much of Europe and harbingers of war in

<color=#3366CC>Scandinavia</color>. In <color=#3366CC>heraldry</color>, birds, especially eagles, often appear in <color=#3366CC>coats of arms</color> In <color=#3366CC>vexillology</color>, birds are a popular
choice on flags. Birds feature in the flag designs of 17 countries and numerous subnational entities and territories. Birds
are used by nations to symbolise a country's identity and heritage, with 91 countries officially recognising a national
bird. Birds of prey are highly represented, though some nations have chosen other species of birds with parrots being
popular among smaller, tropical nations.
In music
In music, birdsong has influenced composers and musicians in several ways: they can be inspired by birdsong; they
can intentionally imitate bird song in a composition, as <color=#3366CC>Vivaldi</color>, <color=#3366CC>Messiaen</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Beethoven</color> did, along with many later
composers; they can incorporate recordings of birds into their works, as <color=#3366CC>Ottorino Respighi</color> first did; or like Beatrice
Harrison and David Rothenberg, they can duet with birds.
A 2023 archaeological excavation of a 10,000-year-old site in Israel yielded hollow wing bones of coots and ducks with
perforations made on the side that are thought to have allowed them to be used as flutes or whistles possibly used by
<color=#3366CC>Natufian</color> people to lure birds of prey.
Threats and conservation
Human activities have caused population decreases or <color=#3366CC>extinction</color> in many bird species. Over a hundred bird species
have gone extinct in historical times, although the most dramatic human-caused avian extinctions, eradicating an
estimated 750–1800 species, occurred during the human colonisation of <color=#3366CC>Melanesian</color>, <color=#3366CC>Polynesian</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Micronesian</color>
islands. Many bird populations are declining worldwide, with 1,227 species listed as threatened by <color=#3366CC>BirdLife International</color>
and the <color=#3366CC>IUCN</color> in 2009. There have been long-term declines in North American bird populations, with an estimated loss
of 2.9 billion breeding adults, about 30% of the total, since 1970.
The most commonly cited human threat to birds is <color=#3366CC>habitat loss</color>. Other threats include overhunting, collisions with
buildings or vehicles, <color=#3366CC>long-line fishing</color> bycatch, pollution (including oil spills and pesticide use), competition and
predation from nonnative <color=#3366CC>invasive species</color>, and climate change.
Governments and <color=#3366CC>conservation</color> groups work to protect birds, either by passing laws that preserve and <color=#3366CC>restore</color> bird
habitat or by establishing captive populations for reintroductions. Such projects have produced some successes; one
study estimated that conservation efforts saved 16 species of bird that would otherwise have gone extinct between
1994 and 2004, including the <color=#3366CC>California condor</color> and Norfolk parakeet.
Human activities have allowed the expansion of a few temperate area species, such as the <color=#3366CC>barn swallow</color> and <color=#3366CC>European</color>
<color=#3366CC>starling</color>. In the tropics and sub-tropics, relatively more species are expanding due to human activities, particularly due
to the spread of crops such as rice whose expansion in south Asia has benefitted at least 64 bird species, though may
have harmed many more species.
